prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are the case in this shortlist where a clean theoretical idea (spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry giving a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states) was followed by an unambiguous experimental signature, the quantized edge conductance in HgTe wells, and then by many independent confirmations in 2D and 3D materials. It opened a genuinely new class of quantum matter, and it has been reproduced across laboratories for about two decades. Four members ranked it in their top three and it is the only candidate ranked by six of eight members, which suggests the support is broad and not an artifact of one subfield. After hearing the colleagues, I move it ahead of my own opening first choice. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible trio that pairs the decisive theory with the first experimental observation, and it extends the 2016 topological-phase prize without duplicating it.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's group tested, and they are outside the credited names. The 3D strand (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy, and Hasan's ARPES work) is arguably a second discovery, and a trio that omits Hasan may be criticised. A fair statement of the discovery may need either a narrower 2D citation or a two-part prize, and the three-person cap makes both uncomfortable. There is also some risk that condensed-matter topology looks like a continuation of 2016 and 2010 (graphene), and several of the materials applications that were promised remain modest.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first because the Z2 mechanism is simple, general and rigorously analysable, the field is mature and textbook, and the prize would extend the 2016 topological-phase prize without duplicating it.
responses.response: I agree and this moved me. I would add the experimental half of the argument, because it is what makes the prize a discovery and not only a classification: the HgTe edge conductance of about 2e^2/h is a clean, quantitative, device-level signature, which is the kind of measurable detail I trust. Where I qualify your view is the trio. You would take the two theorists, but dropping Molenkamp removes the experiment that turned Z2 theory into an observed effect, so I prefer Kane, Mele and Molenkamp over a theory-only pair. I accept that the BHZ credit gap remains and cannot be fully resolved with these names.

responses.point: Danielsson puts IceCube (B005, Halzen alone) first as a clean clue from nature that opened a new observational window, with strong confirmation by the TXS 0506+056 association and the Galactic-plane map, and he ranks topological insulators third with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan.
responses.response: I take the IceCube case seriously and I defer to you and Mark Pearce on detector systematics, since this is outside my field. My hesitation is attribution and not physics: a single-name prize for a cubic-kilometre collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors leaves a visible credit gap, and only the two of you ranked it. On your trio, I would push back gently on replacing Mele with Hasan. Kane and Mele wrote the founding paper together, and Hasan's ARPES work is a separate 3D step. If the committee wants Hasan, it should be a deliberate second part and not a swap that splits the original theory pair.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B034, Katori and Ye) first because they open new observables at the 10^-18 level, such as redshift over millimetres and searches for varying constants, with mature independent confirmation, and he ranks circuit QED only seventh.
responses.response: Your ranking of circuit QED seventh is fair, and I accept it. I will say openly that my own first place for B035 is the choice I should weigh least, given my field and role, and the 2025 prize on circuit macroscopic tunnelling makes a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon hard to defend. I do think the clocks are a strong, clean case and keep B034 as an alternative. My reservation is that they feel closer to a measurement-technology achievement that builds on the 2005 comb prize and on Wineland's ion clocks, so I ask whether the discovery content is a new regime of physics or an extreme refinement. I would like to hear how you separate those.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of quantum matter whose predictions agree with measured spectra, and he flags that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D pioneers are outside the credited list. He ranks twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and with your own flag on attribution, which is the same weakness I list. On twisted bilayer graphene I differ somewhat from your slight preference: the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 result is a lovely theory-experiment pair, but after eight years the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated and Andrei's earlier STM role is unresolved, so I think it is a year or two less settled than topological insulators. I keep it as my first alternative and not as the preferred choice.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and flags that circuit QED may be too close to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so a quantum-circuits prize may not be wanted so soon.
responses.response: I agree with the overlap concern and this is a main reason I have moved off my own opening first place. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit, while circuit QED recognises strong coupling to microwave photons and the readout and architecture that followed, so the scientific steps are distinct. But the optics for a committee that has just rewarded superconducting circuits are poor, and the Girvin and Huang credit question makes the case harder. I would rather revisit circuit QED in a later year than press it now.

uncertainties: Whether a three-person topological-insulator prize can be framed so that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan is acceptable, or whether two parts are needed, which the person limit makes hard.

Whether the committee judges magic-angle graphene sufficiently mature given the unsettled superconducting mechanism, or whether optical lattice clocks have a stronger claim as a clean, reproduced discovery.
How much weight to give the 2016 topological-phase prize when judging whether topological insulators are a sufficiently distinct achievement.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, and Chalmers hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as guest researchers. This is a specific connection to circuit QED (B035), which I ranked first in my opening, so I should recuse myself from any decision on B035. I have no apparent personal or institutional connection to B028, B046, B034, B005 or B011 beyond general scientific acquaintance.
